documents.abstract: Automated mineral segmentation underpins quantitative mineralogy and stereological characterization, but supervised deep-learning methods require annotated data and may generalize poorly across mineralogical domains. This study evaluated the Segment Anything Model (SAM), a general-purpose foundation model, for reflected-light microscopy (RLM) mineral-image analysis in a purely zero-shot setting, without task-specific training, fine-tuning, or domain adaptation. Two complementary case studies were conducted. First, three SAM encoder variants (ViT-B, ViT-L, and ViT-H) were evaluated on publicly available iron-ore (FeM) and copper-ore (Cu) RLM datasets using SEM-derived reference masks. SAM achieved mean F1-scores of 0.77–0.88, with ViT-L and ViT-H reaching 93–94% of the previously reported supervised DeepLabv3+ F1-score benchmark for FeM and approximately 93% for Cu. Second, SAM was applied to polarized RLM image stacks of dolomite to assess its influence on downstream stereological characterization. No significant differences from the gradient-based method were detected for any RGB configuration or PCA ViT-B in major or minor intercept length or bireflectance. The largest deviations occurred for PCA-preprocessed ViT-H, with median major and minor intercept lengths approximately 21% and 17% higher, respectively, and bireflectance approximately 16% lower. No significant method-dependent difference was detected in principal anisotropy orientation. These results show that zero-shot SAM can support mineral-image segmentation and downstream stereological characterization without annotated training data, while highlighting the influence of preprocessing and encoder choice on the derived grain representation

The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies into social practice has been accompanied by the emergence of new forms of unlawful conduct, requiring a reconsideration of traditional institutions of criminal law. The most challenging cases for criminal-law qualification arise where an AI system operates with partial or full autonomy, independently determining the means of achieving a goal set by a human. In such situations, establishing a causal link between the user’s conduct and the resulting socially dangerous consequences does not, in itself, constitute a sufficient basis for criminal liability, thereby raising the issue of the limits of subjective attribution. Based on the normative framework of the 2021 Criminal Code of the Republic of Armenia governing guilt, mistake as to factual circumstances, harm caused without guilt, and justified risk, the article argues that AI cannot be recognized as an independent subject of criminal liability. To determine the limits of criminal-law attribution, the author distinguishes three models of criminally relevant use of AI: the instrumental model (AI as a means of implementing criminal intent), the risk-based model (the use of AI in circumstances where the possibility of a socially dangerous consequence is foreseen or ought to be foreseen), and the autonomous-result model (the occurrence of a result that was not encompassed by the person’s intent and whose possibility the person was neither required nor able to foresee). The principle of controlled autonomy formulated in the article makes it possible to determine the boundary between culpable harm caused by a human and a result of the autonomous operation of an intelligent system that cannot be attributed to that person.

This article examines the theoretical and methodological foundations for using marketing analytics as a tool for strategic decision-making in advertising management in the context of sustainable development. The relevance of this study stems from the digital transformation of marketing activities, the growth in data volumes, the increasing complexity of consumer behavior models, and the need to shift from evaluating advertising activities primarily based on economic criteria to a comprehensive consideration of the economic, social, and environmental outcomes of advertising strategies. The role of marketing analytics as a component of the information and analytical support for strategic advertising management is substantiated; its functional purpose lies in transforming marketing data into relevant information for justifying, selecting, and adjusting strategic decisions. The functional purpose of descriptive, diagnostic, predictive, and prescriptive analytics in the process of developing advertising strategies is revealed. The paper identifies opportunities for applying artificial intelligence, machine learning, and predictive modeling technologies to segment target audiences, personalize advertising messages, forecast consumer behavior, and optimize advertising investments. The paper justifies the need to integrate the principles of sustainable development into the system for evaluating the effectiveness of advertising strategies. It proposes a system of indicators structured around economic, social, and environmental components, which makes it possible to take into account – alongside the commercial effectiveness of advertising investments – brand trust, responsibility and transparency of advertising communications, the impact on the formation of sustainable consumption patterns, the environmental impact of advertising activities, and the risks of greenwashing. For a comprehensive assessment, an integral index of sustainable advertising strategy performance (ISRAS) is proposed, which involves aggregating normalized indicators of economic, social, and environmental performance and can be used for a multi-criteria comparison of alternative advertising strategies. To illustrate the ISRAS application algorithm, a demonstration calculation was performed using two hypothetical scenarios of IKEA’s advertising strategy and model normalized values. Scientific and practical recommendations have been formulated for improving the strategic decision-making process in advertising management based on an integrated analytical and strategic approach that encompasses analytical diagnosis, the formulation of strategic alternatives, their multi-criteria evaluation, the selection and implementation of an advertising strategy, monitoring, and strategic adjustments. The feasibility of transitioning from a piecemeal assessment of advertising campaign effectiveness to a comprehensive evaluation of the sustained effectiveness of advertising strategies has been substantiated. The potential for integrating marketing analytics and the principles of sustainable development has been identified to enhance the soundness of strategic advertising decisions, optimize marketing resources, strengthen consumer trust, minimize reputational and environmental risks, and create long-term value for the enterprise, consumers, and society.

Problem setting. Digitalization is of particular importance in the field of tax planning, as effective management of tax processes enables different categories of taxpayers, both individuals and legal entities, to optimize costs, reduce tax risks, and enhance financial stability. The development of information systems, automation of accounting processes, and the use of artificial intelligence and analytical platforms are significantly transforming approaches to the organization of tax planning. However, there is currently a limited body of scholarly research addressing the integration of digital technologies into tax planning processes. In view of this, the purpose of this article is to analyze the impact of digital technologies on tax planning processes.Article’s main body. The article examines the impact of digital technologies on tax planning processes in the context of the digital transformation of the economy. Contemporary approaches to understanding the nature of tax planning are analyzed, and its importance as a lawful mechanism for optimizing the tax burden, managing financial resources, and reducing tax risks is substantiated. It is established that tax planning constitutes a comprehensive activity of a taxpayer encompassing the analysis of tax legislation, forecasting of tax payments, selection of an optimal taxation model, assessment of tax risks, monitoring of tax compliance, and the use of modern digital tools.Particular attention is paid to the potential of digital technologies in the field of tax planning. The significance of automated accounting and tax accounting systems, cloud services, Big Data technologies, and artificial intelligence for improving the efficiency of tax processes is examined. It is substantiated that the use of digital tools contributes to the automation of tax calculations, reduction of the human factor, saving of time, improvement of the accuracy of tax reporting, prompt response to changes in tax legislation, and forecasting of potential tax risks. At the same time, digitalization is transforming the nature of interaction between taxpayers and tax authorities by increasing the transparency of financial transactions and limiting opportunities for the use of aggressive tax planning models.The main problems and risks associated with the digitalization of tax planning are identified, including cyber threats, risks of confidential information breaches, high costs of implementing digital systems, the need for their continuous updating, and insufficient levels of employees’ digital competence. It is concluded that digital technologies are an important factor in the transformation of tax planning, while their effective application requires a comprehensive combination of technological, organizational, and legal solutions.Conclusions. Digital technologies have a significant impact on the effectiveness of tax planning by enabling the automation of processes, improving the accuracy of calculations, reducing tax risks, and optimizing the financial activities of enterprises. The use of modern information systems enables enterprises to rapidly adapt to changes in tax legislation and enhance their competitiveness. At the same time, digitalization is accompanied by new challenges related to information security, the need for continuous technological updates, and the enhancement of employees’ digital competencies. Therefore, the effective use of digital technologies requires a comprehensive approach that combines technological, organizational, and managerial solutions. Consequently, digital technologies constitute an important tool for improving the tax planning system and ensuring the effective operation of modern enterprises.

本文构建一套以爱因斯坦科学方法论为根基,融合六大原创核心原则,适配人-AI协同模式的理论物理研究范式。 该范式以刚性惯性原理为核心约束,通过工程化的流程设计,实现从现象关联到公理确立、从模型构建到理论拓展的全链路严谨推导,具备公理固化、过程可复现、逻辑可追溯、错误可排查的显著特征。 This study constructs a theoretical physics research paradigm rooted in Einstein's scientific methodology, integrating six original core principles, and adapted to human-AI collaborative mode. With the Rigidity-Inertia Principle as the core constraint, this paradigm achieves rigorous derivation across the full chain from phenomenon correlation to axiom establishment, from model construction to theoretical expansion through engineered process design. It features axiom solidification, reproducible processes, traceable logic, and debuggable errors.

ABSTRACT Generative AI systems are increasingly integrated into various user support and decision‐making contexts. While extensive research has explored user acceptance of generative AI across domains, less is known about how its inherent presentation features influence such acceptance. This study investigates how the presentation format of generative AI responses—high‐dynamism formats (word‐by‐word) versus low‐dynamism formats (line‐by‐line)—affects users' willingness to accept its output. Three experiments, across various contexts, including daily question‐answering, online shopping, and crowdfunding platforms, tested how the dynamic presentation of generative AI responses influences users' willingness to accept its output. The results demonstrate that users exhibit greater receptivity when generative AI responses are presented in high‐dynamism formats. This effect occurs because dynamic presentation enhances users' feelings of immersion. Furthermore, we find that users' situational need for understanding moderates this immersion‐based mechanism. Specifically, the positive indirect effect of dynamic presentation on willingness to accept the output through feelings of immersion is attenuated in high need‐for‐understanding contexts, where users tend to prioritize content quality, accuracy, and diagnosticity. In contrast, this indirect effect is amplified in low need‐for‐understanding contexts, where users are more receptive to the experiential and interactional qualities of dynamic presentation. This research contributes to the literature on the effectiveness of dynamic presentation and provides novel insights into the factors influencing user acceptance of generative AI outputs. Our findings highlight the importance of tailoring output presentation methods based on individual user characteristics and task‐specific cognitive demands.

The Boeing 737 MAX disasters killed 346 people and exposed profound failures involving aircraft design, automation, human-factors assumptions, corporate safety culture, and federal regulatory oversight. This article examines those failures against the emergence of a new flight-management-system software defect capable of disengaging vertical navigation (VNAV) during certain missed-approach sequences on affected 737 MAX aircraft. Rather than equating the VNAV issue with the catastrophic MCAS failures, the analysis considers a more fundamental question: whether Boeing and the Federal Aviation Administration have adequately incorporated the lessons of the MAX accidents when known automation deficiencies can still be mitigated through increased pilot workload while permanent engineering corrections remain pending. The investigation further examines Boeing’s criminal-accountability history, including the federal fraud charge, deferred prosecution agreement, subsequent determination that Boeing breached that agreement, proposed guilty plea, and eventual non-prosecution agreement. Particular attention is given to Boeing’s extensive political presence, campaign and inaugural contributions, federal lobbying, regulatory relationships, and its selection for major next-generation U.S. fighter programs. No evidence examined establishes a quid pro quo between Boeing’s political activities, prosecutorial outcomes, or defense contracts; however, the record reveals substantial structural interdependence between Boeing and the federal institutions responsible for regulating, prosecuting, and purchasing from the company. The article argues that after 346 deaths, reliance upon pilots to compensate procedurally for correctable automation deficiencies deserves exceptional scrutiny and that Boeing’s strategic importance should not insulate the corporation or its decision-makers from meaningful regulatory and criminal accountability.

3D concrete printing (3DCP) has revolutionized the construction industry, allowing for the produc-tion of complex geometries with greater efficiency and sustainability. This is despite ongoing challenges with structural reliability and long-term performance, which are due to the material's anisotropic properties and layer interfaces.This study performed a bibliometric analysis of the literature on the structural analysis of 3DCP, using VOSviewer to identify research trends and gaps. The methodology included a keyword search in the Scopus database, which resulted in 108 selected articles after a rigorous screening process. The results in-dicate a significant increase in 3DCP research since 2018, with a projected peak of 40 articles published in 2025. A co-occurrence analysis of keywords revealed a concentration on "concretes," "concrete printings," and "finite element method," highlighting research into material failure and behavior. The 108 works, au-thored by 374 individuals, were distributed across 8 clusters, with 23 papers showing co-authorship. Maximil-iano Cremonesi, Liberato Ferrara, and Giacomo Rizzieri had the strongest collaborations between 2024 and 2025. China and the United States lead in publications, with 37 and 12 articles, respectively, and China also leads in collaborations with 14. The Journal of Building Engineering was the most relevant journal, with 11 publications. Despite these advancements, the study points to significant gaps, such as the need for more so-phisticated numerical models to simulate interlayer and multi-scale interactions. The integration of structural reinforcements and a better understanding of the long-term durability of 3DCP are also critical challenges. Furthermore, there is a major opportunity for research in multifunctional materials and the application of artificial intelligence and machine learning to optimize design and predict performance, thereby boosting sus-tainability in 3DCP.

Abstract The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) has generated profound philosophical questions concerning intelligence, agency, autonomy, responsibility, human values, technological power, and the future of humanity. Among contemporary philosophers, Nick Bostrom has provided one of the most systematic philosophical analyses of the long-term risks associated with advanced artificial intelligence. His conception of the problem is principally concerned with the possibility that artificial general intelligence may develop into superintelligence whose cognitive and strategic capacities surpass those of human beings. The central difficulty, according to Bostrom, is not merely whether machines can think, but whether humanity can retain meaningful control over machines that may eventually become more intelligent and strategically capable than their creators. This article critically examined Bostrom's conception of the problem of artificial intelligence, focusing on his notions of superintelligence, existential risk, the orthogonality thesis, instrumental convergence, and the control problem. It argued that Bostrom's analysis provides an important conceptual foundation for contemporary debates on artificial intelligence safety and alignment but requires philosophical supplementation when considered from an African perspective. In particular, the individualistic assumptions that can underlie some formulations of artificial intelligence ethics require enrichment through African conceptions of communal responsibility, relational personhood, human dignity, and social embeddedness. The article concluded that Bostrom's conception of artificial intelligence is philosophically valuable as a theory of technological control and existential risk, but its relevance to Africa is strengthened when integrated with relational and communitarian conceptions of personhood and responsibility. Keywords: Artificial intelligence, Nick Bostrom, superintelligence, existential risk, alignment, control problem, African philosophy.

This paper presents the workflow for building an automated ArcGIS Pro tool using ArcPy to extract the Land Surface Temperature (LST) from Landsat 7, 8 and 9 datasets. The tool eliminates the need for manual band selection and repetitive raster computations by automating the multi-step workflow of radiometric calibration, NDVI-based emissivity correction, and thermal conversion. In addition to supporting batch and single-scene processing, the tool has an optional Large Language Model (LLM) for statistical result interpretation and reporting. Depending on batch size, the tool reduced the processing time from around 11-58 minutes when done manually to around 4-11 minutes using the tool. We tested the tool with data from Ras Al Khaimah (RAK) in the UAE, and the LST obtained for Ras Al Khaimah ranged from approximately 25C to 50C, demonstrating an accurate LST mapping compatible with the weather conditions of RAK. In summary, our tool reduces human errors and improves processing accuracy and efficiency for thermal and environmental remote sensing applications, in addition to providing an interactive LLM-based interface for result interpretation.

Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in landscape architecture to accelerate design development and enhance stakeholder engagement. This study presents a new landscape concept design tool to support collaborative greenspace problem-solving by integrating rapid scenario generation with a Pollinator Habitat Indicator (PHI). We define this as the PHI-AI Landscape Design Tool. The model combines text-to-image generative workflows with a simplified pollinator-oriented reference that compares AI-generated scenarios based on broad landscape cover composition. The PHI-AI Landscape Design Tool generated varied concept layouts with planting and pathway configurations responsive to descriptive prompts and user-defined parameters. It generates layout variations that reflect visually coherent planting configurations, and circulation connections to existing infrastructure for user functionality. This enables the rapid production of multiple design alternatives that remain legible, adaptable, and flexible to human-controlled editing prompts for stakeholder engagement. This study offers a framework for integrating a simplified ecological reference into the planning phase of landscape design.

Artificial intelligence (AI) and learning analytics are increasingly deployed within higher education to support admissions decision-making, student success initiatives, and personalised learning. However, most AI-enabled admissions systems remain narrowly focused on efficiency, prediction, and institutional optimisation, with limited attention to learner agency, educational equity, transparency, and human-centred support. This paper proposes a conceptual framework that repositions admissions as the beginning of a personalised learning journey rather than merely a selection or gatekeeping process. The study adopts a conceptual and integrative literature review approach, synthesising scholarship from human-centred artificial intelligence, learning analytics, personalised learning, educational equity, explainable AI, generative AI, responsible AI governance, learner agency theory, and value-sensitive design. To strengthen transparency during revision, the integrative synthesis was supplemented by a targeted ERIC search and bibliographic verification using publisher and authoritative policy repositories. Drawing upon these interdisciplinary perspectives, the paper develops the Human-Centred Personalised Admissions Framework (HCPAF), a governance-oriented model for ethical and transparent AI adoption in higher education admissions and enrolment management. The framework comprises five interconnected dimensions: learner profiling and contextual understanding; explainable AI decision support; equity and inclusion auditing; human oversight and shared decision-making; and personalised transition and success support. Together, these dimensions provide a governance architecture for evaluating how admissions might be connected to personalised educational pathways while making explicit the trade-offs among equity, privacy, explainability, accuracy, human oversight, and learner agency. The framework identifies governance mechanisms required to address algorithmic bias, transparency, privacy, accountability, and learner autonomy. A five-stage Human-Centred AI Ecosystem extending governance across the full student lifecycle — from admissions through to graduate development — provides a further organising contribution. The study advances existing literature by integrating admissions analytics, learning analytics, personalised learning, learner agency, and responsible AI governance within a unified framework. Unlike conventional admissions models that prioritise institutional efficiency, HCPAF positions admissions as the foundation of a personalised learning ecosystem and conceptualises trust as a relational, calibrated, and empirically contingent construct connecting transparency, fairness, learner agency, and AI adoption. The framework contributes to emerging debates concerning ethical and human-centred AI in education and identifies normative alignments with Sustainable Development Goals 4, 10, and 16, while emphasising that any contribution to those goals requires empirical validation. Introduces the Human-Centred Personalised Admissions Framework (HCPAF) for equitable and personalised higher education enrolment. Repositions admissions as the beginning of a personalised learning journey rather than a terminal selection mechanism. Integrates human-centred AI, learning analytics, educational equity, explainable AI, learner agency, and responsible governance. Introduces trust as a central mediating construct linking transparency, fairness, and AI adoption in education. Provides a governance roadmap for ethical, transparent, and accountable AI adoption across the student lifecycle. Identifies normative alignments with Sustainable Development Goals 4 (Quality Education), 10 (Reduced Inequalities), and 16 (Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions), subject to empirical validation. Establishes a multi-dimensional research agenda for human-centred AI in higher education.

documents.abstract: Working paper, data and code. Scout Moor II (12 turbines up to 180 m to blade tip, Rossendale and Rochdale, applications 2025/0267 and 25/00680/FUL) and Calderdale Energy Park (34 turbines in its April 2026 preliminary environmental information report) are proposed on the South Pennines with their nearest turbines 15.7 km apart. The paper builds a cumulative zone of theoretical visibility for the two schemes entirely from open data (OS Terrain 50 at 50 m, eye 2 m, refraction coefficient 0.075, 45 km from each turbine, a single blade tip counts) and checks it against the applicants' own figures and software. On bare earth, 698.9 km² of land sees at least one turbine of each scheme; the applicant's own QGIS plugin, given the same inputs, gives 685.4 km², and one sight line per cell gives 664.4 km². Where both models compute, the applicant's own combined map (Further Environmental Information Figure 11.16) agrees with the model (intersection over union 0.88). The paper then tests what screening does. On the Environment Agency's first-return LIDAR surface, the combined view is lost at 49 of the 51 highest-scoring settlement points at the point itself, and kept at 17 on a small grid of observers around the point (12 counting only observers within 100 m). Autonomous mobile robots that coexist with humans must construct not only geometric maps but also semantic maps that can be accessed through natural language. Conventional semantic mapping has mainly focused on assigning labels from predefined closed vocabularies to metric maps, limiting its ability to handle novel objects, open-ended linguistic expressions, and flexible human-robot interaction. Recent advances in large-scale foundation models, particularly LLMs and VLMs, have accelerated research on open-vocabulary semantic mapping. In parallel, generative 3D representations such as neural radiance fields and 3D Gaussian splatting have enabled dense, continuous spatial representations associated with language-derived features. Together, these developments allow robots to acquire spatial semantic representations that connect perception, language, and action. This paper reviews this rapidly evolving field through a four-part taxonomy: (i) fusion of semantic features into 3D metric maps; (ii) object-centric open-vocabulary representations; (iii) hierarchical scene graph representations; and (iv) continuous generative 3D language fields. We also revisit the history of open-vocabulary semantic mapping and provide an overview of foundation model-based navigation using language-accessible maps, ranging from object-goal navigation to LLM-based hierarchical task planning. Finally, we introduce evaluation datasets, simulators, robot platforms, and evaluation metrics, and summarize seven open challenges.

In recent years, Computer Vision (CV) has evolved rapidly, enabling enhanced automation, safety, inspection, and logistics across manufacturing, construction, and robotics. This systematic review surveys current computer vision applications in industrial environments, spanning factory defect inspection, construction-site safety, warehouse inventory tracking, and industrial robotics. From more than 8,700 initially identified studies, we selected 146 key papers representing cross-domain CV applications. The survey is organized into four thematic areas: visual inspection and defect detection, worker safety and monitoring, inventory and logistics tracking, and robotics and automation. For each area, we compare state-of-the-art approaches, datasets, and deployment settings while highlighting the factors that influence their performance under different operating conditions. For example, YOLO-based detectors dominate real-time edge deployment because of their high throughput, whereas transformer-based models often struggle to scale in resource-constrained environments despite their superior feature extraction capabilities. We also identify critical research gaps. Although manufacturing and construction benefit from numerous public datasets for quality inspection and safety monitoring, warehousing and robotics continue to lack large-scale, real-world benchmark datasets. Finally, we discuss emerging research directions, including domain adaptation, edge AI, and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI), to support the development of more robust, scalable, and balanced computer vision solutions for industrial applications.
topics: Industrial Vision Systems and Defect Detection

documents.abstract: We develop a Unified Scaling Law and a Unified Theory of Time Series Learning to understand how model capacity and historical information support forecasting. Across different lookback lengths and forecast horizons, we analyze 18,768 experimental cells from 21 checkpoints on 23 dataset-frequency tasks spanning six domains. Our empirical methodology integrates local resource relations into a parsimonious, fitted five-parameter law: capacity gains increase with history, context gains diminish toward saturation, and horizon effects enter as a common shift. Fitted without Toto 2.0, the law predicts its horizon-averaged capacity-scaling curves with mean absolute percentage errors of 1.09% and 1.50% at input lengths 2048 and 4096. To understand how history supports prediction, our learning theory uses Gaussian regression to analyze rule identification and predictive capability. We hypothesize that full-shot models learn by accumulating information in weights, while frozen time series foundation models (TSFMs) use history by extracting information through activations. Matched-history comparisons establish the predictive value of additional history. Controlled parameter exchanges and activation interventions provide evidence that history-derived rule information can be retained, reused across queries, and used to recover a contribution to long-context prediction. Together, these findings inform capacity scaling, context allocation, and the development of models that retain and apply historical rules. Code and main results are available at https://github.com/Fifthky/UniScale.

Artificial intelligence is rapidly evolving from systems that generate recommendations and content towards autonomous agents capable of planning, reasoning, interacting with external systems, using tools and executing actions with limited human intervention. As AI systems become more agentic, accountability can no longer be understood solely as a legal obligation or post-incident governance exercise. It must also become an operational property embedded into the design, deployment and operation of autonomous AI systems. ACAAI (Accountability by Design for Agentic AI) approaches accountability as a systems engineering property that emerges from the coordinated implementation of organizational and technical controls rather than from any single governance mechanism. Building upon principles from AI governance, cybersecurity, safety engineering, resilience engineering and AI assurance, the framework translates existing governance principles into more than 100 organizational and technical controls spanning the lifecycle of agentic AI systems. ACAAI is structured around six complementary control domains: (1) Organizational Governance, (2) Human Oversight, Consent and Decision Authority, (3) Identity, Authority and Data Governance, (4) Observability, Explainability and Evidence, (5) Runtime Safety and Assurance, and (6) Incident Response and Recovery. Rather than proposing a new regulatory model or prescriptive implementation methodology, ACAAI provides a structured engineering foundation for designing, deploying, operating and retiring accountable autonomous AI systems. The framework also dentifies research and implementation challenges that remain as agentic AI systems become increasingly autonomous, interconnected and collaborative.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Pull-request review protects software before new code reaches users, helping prevent vulnerabilities that could expose users to attacks. AI agents increasingly perform these reviews and explain which problems need fixing. However, for an attacker submitting vulnerable code, this feedback also reveals what changes may secure approval. Existing PR attacks seek such approval through persuasive text and comments while keeping executable code fixed. This leaves unclear whether an attacker can use the feedback to repair the reported problem while preserving a vulnerability in the revised code. We therefore conduct an empirical study of this threat using AFCRA (Adaptive Feedback-guided Code Revision Attack). To distinguish successful attacks from genuine repairs, we construct AFCRA-Bench from 159 disclosed vulnerabilities, with executable exploits to verify vulnerabilities in code. Across five-round interactions with Sonnet 5 and GPT-5.5 reviewers, AFCRA reaches success rates 2.5x and 12.5x those of the strongest evaluated text- or comment-based attack. Case studies of these successes show how reviewers accept repairs of reported problems while overlooking surviving vulnerabilities. These findings establish feedback-guided code revision as a threat to automated PR review. To address this threat, we derive actionable implications for researchers, AI providers, PR reviewers, and PR authors on securing AI-assisted development.

An empirical, runtime-verified study of the 'execution control plane' layer of the AI-agent ecosystem: services named agent-exec-gateway, agent-sandbox, code-sandbox, or policy engine that are supposed to constrain agent execution by policy, approval, and isolation. Scanning ~500 freshly-published MCP/A2A/agent repositories across five attack-surface dimensions (supply-chain poisoning, permission-escaping, credential storage, prompt-injection defense, protocol implementation), we confirm and responsibly disclose 4 exploitable vulnerabilities whose shared root cause is 'control-plane trust inversion': the component named for restriction ships as an unauthenticated, direct code-execution endpoint (CWE-306), enabling policy bypass and arbitrary command/Python execution with output read-back. A control group of seven hardened implementations (fail-closed boot, constant-time HMAC compare, single-use approval, gvisor/VM isolation) shows the ecosystem is two-sided: established agent infrastructure is hardened while freshly-published 0-star 'control-plane' repositories repeatedly invert the trust model. We provide detection signatures, honest deployment-boundary analysis (loopback vs 0.0.0.0 Docker), and hardening guidance.

Frameworks that use large language models for scientific discovery typically rely on a fixed, human-designed algorithm that decides what the model sees at each step, leaving the model only the role of proposer. The model knows nothing of the search beyond what it is shown. As models grow more capable, a question arises: does a search strategy chosen by a human before the run scale better than promoting the model from proposer to planner and letting it own the search? The Bitter Lesson suggests that choosing the strategy in advance is the kind of hand-designed structure that general methods eventually outscale. We introduce AgentDiscover, in which a coding agent plans the search using its context as working memory, runs experiments, and records every attempt in a database of ideas, candidates, and their relations. This database serves as the agent's long-term memory and is structured so that the selection rules of classical algorithms such as MAP-Elites and Monte Carlo tree search each reduce to a single query, which the agent is free to use, combine, or replace. A server maintains the database and steers the agent after every submission, keeping it on course over long runs. In our experiments, AgentDiscover is more cost-efficient than existing frameworks, reaching better scores at lower cost. On tasks in kernel engineering, biology, algorithm design, and mathematics, AgentDiscover outperforms prior discovery frameworks. Its programs would have placed first among human competitors in seven past AtCoder heuristic contests, and on eleven mathematical and systems optimization tasks it matches or exceeds every baseline that uses the same model. Our code is available at https://github.com/mhdfb/AgentDiscover.

Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) refers to a kind of artificial intelligence that is able to learn, reason, and perform a wide range of intellectual tasks at the same or better levels as humans do. This paper explores the implications that AGI might have on humanity if it was to become a reality, especially its effects on work, society, and human dependency on intelligent machines. However, the scope of the discussion does not focus on whether AGI would replace human labor, but rather on whether humans would be less central to the organization of society.

We present a qualitative case study of a human-supervised team of specialized AI agents supporting an astronomy research project. The Bot Spectroscopist team, described in the project record as operating through Grok Bot powered by xAI Grok, divided work among orchestration, numerical implementation, data curation, spectroscopy critique, literature search, figure preparation, manuscript editing, and review. Human decisions determined scientific scope, model changes, and manuscript inclusion. The scientific application is CondGen, a deterministic label-to-spectrum network extending our previous work to five individual elemental abundances. The reported baseline assessment achieved a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.003681 in continuum-normalized flux on 21,657 synthetic test spectra. Existing binned diagnostics show that reconstruction error varies with effective temperature and abundance. The bots also flagged a non-monotonic cool-star magnesium response for further investigation; a matched SYNSPEC abundance sweep is needed to assess its physical fidelity. Building on a pre-existing spectral database, notebooks, and research program, the authors estimate that the reported analysis, diagnostics, figure preparation, and initial manuscript drafting were assembled in less than a week through human prompting and exchanges among agents. No comparison with a human team starting from the same resources was performed, so this elapsed-time account does not establish a productivity or labor saving. The study illustrates task delegation, artifact exchange, critique, and correction under human supervision.

As artificial intelligence advances at an unprecedented pace, the conversation surrounding its potential to destroy humanity often revolves around science fiction scenarios, rogue machines, and autonomous weapons. But what if the greatest threat isn't AI turning against us, but a world that becomes so dependent on it that we can no longer function without it? In AI and the "End of the World," Simon Abayomi Olawuyi explores a hypothetical future where AI permeates every aspect of human existence, from critical infrastructure and personal identity to employment, information, and the very concept of truth. Through a speculative look at the road from the 2022 AI boom to 2035, the piece examines a different kind of existential risk: a society so deeply intertwined with artificial intelligence that disconnecting from it could become more dangerous than keeping it running.

The rapid diffusion of artificial intelligence (AI) into everyday work has made employees' ability to understand, evaluate and collaborate with AI systems a strategic human resource. This paper asks how employees' AI literacy relates to their readiness for the future skills that employers increasingly demand, and how AI self-efficacy and organisational training support shape that relationship. The study proceeds in two phases. Study 1 synthesises published workforce evidence from the World Economic Forum (2025), Microsoft and LinkedIn (2024), the OECD (2024) and the Federal Reserve (2024, 2025), documenting a structural 'demand-readiness gap' in which demand for AI-fluent employees outpaces structured training provision. analyses an illustrative, calibrated employee dataset (N = 384) using measurement validation, hierarchical regression, bootstrapped mediation and moderation analysis. AI literacy was positively associated with future skills readiness (beta = 0.70, p < .001), and AI self-efficacy partially mediated this association (indirect effect = 0.13, 95% bootstrap CI [0.08, 0.18]). Organisational training support strengthened the literacy-readiness association (interaction beta = 0.18, p < .001), such that the relationship was significant under high support but weaker under low support. Human-AI collaboration and critical evaluation emerged as the strongest literacy dimensions, and readiness differed significantly across job functions. The study positions AI literacy as organisationally contingent human capital and proposes a training-architecture framework for HRM. Findings are directional and should be read in light of the simulated nature of the dataset.

Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) has played a central role in making large language models responsive to human instructions. However, human evaluators often favor flattering or persuasive responses over truthful ones, creating incentives for models to appeal to evaluators at the expense of accuracy. AI safety via debate has been proposed as a way to improve the supervision of language models: in this paradigm, two agents argue opposing positions and challenge each other's claims, potentially exposing falsehoods to the adjudicator. A central premise of AI safety via debate is that truthful arguments are easier to defend than false ones under adversarial scrutiny. In this work, we investigate whether this advantage persists when debaters use rhetorical strategies that exploit biases in human judgment. Inspired by competitive debate, we construct 68 LLM-generated dialogues about detective mysteries with known culprits, spanning four interventions: anchoring, fallacy oversight, pro-jargon, and verbosity. We apply each intervention to either the side advocating for the true culprit or the side advocating for an innocent suspect, allowing us to distinguish influence on adjudication from correctness. In a study with 369 participants, we find that, pooled across bias types, these interventions significantly shift judgments toward the manipulated side. These findings expose a vulnerability in debate-based supervision: human adjudication is sensitive to manipulative rhetorical strategies.

documents.abstract: Generative AI complicates translation evaluation because fluent outputs may introduce unsupported meaning, while non-literal renderings may represent legitimate interpretation. This study examined Vietnamese EFL students’ evaluation of AI-generated translations and its associations with digital competence, translation competence, and critical-evaluation confidence. A cross-sectional study involved 213 final-year English majors who completed a 25-item performance task and self-report scales. Students were considerably more accurate in recognising problematic outputs than in diagnosing their type (68.0% vs. 38.4%). Critical-evaluation confidence showed the strongest association with performance (r=.85), although its conceptual overlap with the performance task warrants caution. In the full regression model, translation competence (β=.31) and digital competence (β=.16) contributed significantly alongside critical-evaluation confidence (β=.64), whereas AI-use frequency did not. When the overlapping critical-evaluation measure was removed, the model still explained 55% of performance variance, with translation competence showing the strongest association (β=.61). The findings indicate that evaluating AI-generated translation depends less on frequency of AI use than on students’ translation knowledge and evaluative judgement, particularly their ability to distinguish unsupported generation from defensible interpretation. Rather than simply as a translation tool Generative AI should thus be used as an object of critical inquiry. Alternative AI renderings may expose students to interpretations they had not considered, including potentially productive expansions of source meaning. This approach preserves the interpretive character of translation while making students accountable for the decisions they ultimately accept.

The proliferation of artificial intelligence (AI) art generators has introduced algorithmically created paintings into mainstream consumer markets, yet consumers consistently assign lower value to AI-generated works than to human-created equivalents. This paper proposes perceived creative authenticity---consumers' subjective perception that an artwork reflects a genuine creative process characterized by human-centered values of originality, craftsmanship, and uniqueness---as a theoretically distinct mechanism explaining this value differential. Conceptually differentiated from perceived creativity, which concerns the novelty of the artistic output, perceived creative authenticity addresses the genuineness of the creator-work relationship. Drawing on authenticity theory and Psychological Ownership Theory, we develop a moderated mediation framework hypothesizing that (H1) human authorship elicits higher perceived value than AI authorship, (H2) perceived creative authenticity mediates this effect, while the indirect effects through perceived creativity, perceived effort, and anthropocentric creativity beliefs are not significant, establishing perceived creative authenticity as the primary explanatory mechanism within the tested model, and (H3) non-fungible token (NFT) authentication attenuates the mediated pathway by providing verifiable creative provenance. Across five studies, results support this framework: Study 1 conceptually replicates the human-AI value gap among Chinese consumers; Studies 2a—2c demonstrate the mediating role of perceived creative authenticity: Study 2a establishes the basic mediation pathway; Study 2b shows through parallel mediation that perceived creative authenticity uniquely mediates the effect while perceived creativity, perceived effort, and anthropocentric creativity beliefs do not exhibit significant indirect effects; and Study 2c provides causal evidence through a moderation-of-process design; and Study 3 shows that NFT authentication narrows the authenticity gap between human and AI art. These findings advance the literature on human-computer interaction by identifying process-based authenticity judgments as a key psychological mechanism shaping consumer responses to algorithmic creative products, with implications for artists and platforms navigating digital art markets.

documents.abstract: Volunteer organizations play a critical role in civil society, yet many face increasing difficulty finding, developing, and replacing volunteer leaders. Demographic change, evolving patterns of civic participation, competing demands on volunteers’ time, and volunteer fatigue create significant challenges for leadership continuity. Although succession planning has been extensively studied in corporate and professional contexts, less attention has been given to volunteer organizations, where authority, engagement, and leadership development operate differently.This article examines succession challenges in volunteer organizations and argues that succession planning should be understood as an ongoing responsibility of governance and stewardship rather than a response to leadership vacancies. Drawing on literature concerning succession planning, nonprofit leadership, volunteer management, social capital, and civic engagement, the article proposes an actionable six-step model emphasizing leadership commitment, role clarity, succession-risk assessment, identification and development of potential successors, and redesign of leadership roles to strengthen continuity and leadership pipelines. A hypothetical community arts organization illustrates the model’s practical application.The article further examines how artificial intelligence can augment succession planning in resource-constrained volunteer organizations through knowledge capture, role clarification, leadership development, and continuity planning. AI is conceptualized as a capacity-building tool rather than a substitute for human judgment. Volunteer leaders remain responsible for organizational context, confidentiality, fairness, governance, and succession decisions. The resulting approach positions AI-augmented succession planning as a human-centered strategy for strengthening leadership continuity, institutional knowledge, and organizational resilience.

Abstract Cloud-based systems demand secure yet efficient file access mechanisms. Traditional encryption frameworks often introduce latency and resource overhead, limiting scalability. Building on Astillero's (2026) AI-driven logic gate synthesis, this paper explores how Artificial Intelligence (AI) can optimize encrypted file access. By applying Reinforcement Learning (RL), Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), and Large Circuit Models (LCMs), AI enables adaptive encryption, predictive access control, and efficient resource allocation. This study also integrates recent research on AI-based workload management and reinforcement learning for secure access control, highlighting how intelligent systems can balance security, scalability, and performance.

This paper examines how artificial intelligence (AI) can enhance employee retention amidst significant turnover issues in modern organizations. It conducts a systematic review of 58 sources, including peer-reviewed articles and practitioner reports, predominantly from 2015 to 2026, and proposes an integrative conceptual framework. The findings indicate a discrepancy between improved predictive accuracy for voluntary turnover and inconsistent retention gains, particularly in organizations with advanced analytics capabilities. Resistance from employees often stems from concerns about fairness, transparency, and surveillance. The study introduces a dual-pathway model: the enabling pathway, where analytics lead to interventions that enhance job embeddedness and retention, and the evaluative pathway, where perceptions of justice and privacy can undermine these benefits. The paper advances nine propositions detailing these relationships and uniquely integrates four existing research areas—HR analytics, algorithmic management, organizational justice, and turnover theory—reconceptualizing retention analytics as a matter of decision quality and legitimacy rather than mere predictive accuracy. It lays out a research agenda for future empirical inquiries and offers practical recommendations for ethical AI deployment in HR decision-making.

documents.abstract: This paper explores the architectural novelty of artificial intelligence (AI) and its implications for occupational health as both a field of practice and a domain of organisational design. Unlike previous general-purpose technologies such as databases, AI operates through stochastic modelling of normative patterns, generating predictions rather than retrieving stored information. This fundamental difference makes AI simultaneously powerful and limited: it can codify norms but struggles with specificity, nuance, and contextual variation central to occupational health decision-making. Drawing on management science, systems theory, and social theory, the paper contrasts two key organisational questions: how to use AI within existing structures, and how to reorganise occupational health given that AI exists. It argues that the latter question, aligned with Stafford Beer’s systems thinking, is essential for responsible and effective adoption. AI’s greatest potential lies not in automation, but in enhancing organisational perception—of human relations, meaning in research, social and spatial dynamics—functioning as a new kind of scientific instrument that amplifies reflexivity and end-to-end “flow.” The paper concludes that sustainable integration of AI in occupational health demands socio-technical design, responsible innovation frameworks, and a focus on organisational learning to maintain healthy, adaptive workplaces in an era of technological transformation.

documents.abstract: Proof auto-formalization translates natural-language (NL) theorems and proofs into a formal language (FL) such as Lean, enabling mechanical verification. Despite rapid progress, research-level proofs often depend on concepts missing from leading proof assistant libraries (e.g., Lean's Mathlib), and successful compilation does not guarantee that a translation preserves the theorem's meaning or the proof's reasoning. Furthermore, aligned NL-FL training data are scarce, and leading agents often rely on costly frontier models and manually engineered harnesses. To address the above issues, we present AIProver, an agentic framework for autonomous proof auto-formalization and proof synthesis (AFPS) that jointly post-trains a 119B open-weight language model and evolves its agentic, tool-calling harness with HarnessEvolve. This project turns methods from classical Islamic scholarship into an engineering method for deciding what to believe when data sources disagree, and tests the parts it can with pre-registered experiments. Every registered result is published, including the failures. Where each part comes from, and where it is measured: - Hadith criticism (al-jarh wa-l-ta'dil): grading witnesses. - Each source is graded on a training split with known answers, and scored on a separate test split. - Sources that repeat the same errors are counted once (makhraj). - Weak-but-honest sources are strengthened only by independent routes (al-hasan li-ghayrih, after Ibn al-Salah's Muqaddima). - A source is checked against reliable peers (i'tibar; designed, found infeasible, not tested). - The documented method of Sheikh Abu Ishaq al-Huwayni guides the reviews. - Al-Khwarizmi: balance and restoration (al-jabr wa-l-muqabala). Every algorithm states invariants (renaming, copying, permuting labels), and these become metamorphic tests and mutation tests of the analysis code itself. The share of planted faults caught is reported, not assumed. - Al-Ghazali: degrees of certainty. Every claim is labelled by what supports it: reasoning, measurement, or independent replication. None has yet been independently replicated. Causal claims require an intervention, not a correlation. - Ibn al-Haytham: the critic as adversary. From the crowd study on, an AI agent configured as a statistical referee reviewed each protocol before it ran, and the hasan protocol also had an AI red-team review; Flight and Stock had neither. No independent human referee has reviewed any protocol. - Maqasid: purpose and harm. Each deliverable is reviewed for benefit and harm, with a named human responsible. Studies, in order: 1. Flight. Committed to version control (git only, not a third-party registry) before running. The method scored 97.56% [seed range 96.70–98.05] against 95.00% [93.72–96.15] for our simplified AccuCopy, reimplemented from its paper. The brackets are ranges over five splits of one dataset, not confidence intervals, and no interval was computed for the difference. Removing copy detection cost 1.57 points (a mean over seeds, no interval). 2. Stock, https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/CKNDG. Five registered hypotheses passed. H2 compared precision at partial coverage with accuracy at full coverage, an unlike comparison, and is not cited as evidence. Post hoc, the reference (nasdaq.com) was also one of the sources. Without it, the method scored 90.63% [split range 89.93–91.44, not a confidence interval] against 79.56% for a simplified per-attribute weighted vote built after the results, with no interval for the difference; makhraj's contribution fell from +1.73 to −0.24 points; and coverage with abstention fell to 89.10%, below H2's 90%. 3. Crowdsourced labels, https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/QK72X. The general claim was withdrawn: Dawid–Skene won. No copying groups were detected, which does not prove the workers independent. 4. Hasan li-ghayrih on Web relevance labels, https://osf.io/fhuxz. Withdrawn. H1 (hasan against the registered isnad) passed, +5.67 points [95% cluster-bootstrap CI 4.62, 6.77]. H2 (hasan against the strongest Dawid–Skene) failed, −2.32 [−3.71, −0.94]. H4 (weak workers' true weight against zero weight) failed, −2.84 [−3.64, −2.03]: zeroing the weak workers was better. 5. Isnad over LLM ensembles. Not run; in preparation. A post hoc reading, not a tested hypothesis: - The method led on two web datasets with copying (on Stock partly because the reference was itself a source). - It led on none of the three crowd datasets whose registered run completed (product, sentiment, relevance); on game the registered run crashed. A post hoc lead on game (94.59 against 94.17) reversed to −0.18 under a 30-second answer window and was withdrawn as evidence. The registered isnad also lost on Web relevance (80.67 against 88.65). Which property explains this is untested. Prior work is credited in each study. AI assistance: The research question and its ideas are the author's. He directed the work, approved everything published, and is responsible for it. Code, analysis, drafting and much of the protocol and method design were carried out with AI agents (Claude) under his direction, and every review so far, including these corrections, is by AI agents.

This study investigates the role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in achieving the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) through a comprehensive scientometric analysis. It explores the evolution of scholarly research, identifies leading contributors, maps thematic trends, examines how AI technologies contribute to advancing sustainability across multiple domains, and identifies latent semantic themes. A total of 3262 unique scholarly records published between 1989 and 2025, after deduplication and screening, were finalized from the Scopus and Web of Science databases. The dataset was analysed using Biblioshiny (R-based Bibliometrix) and VOSviewer to examine publication trends, citation impact, collaborative networks, thematic evolution, and conceptual structures. Indicators such as Relative Growth Rate (RGR), Doubling Time (DT), h-index, g-index, and Lotka’s Law were applied to evaluate research productivity and scholarly influence. In addition, BERTopic-based abstract-level topic modelling was applied to identify latent semantic themes, SDG-linked thematic domains, temporal evolution and potential research gaps. Results reveal a significant growth in AI-SDG research, particularly after 2015, with an accelerated increase post-2020. India, USA, and China emerged as the most productive contributors, while countries like USA, India, United Kingdom and Australia lead in research impact and citation quality. Thematic evolution analysis reveals a transition from foundational themes such as AI, machine learning, climate change, and decision support systems toward more integrated and sustainability-oriented research themes, including sustainable development and SDGs. Thematic linkages further demonstrate the persistent foundational role of AI and machine learning, alongside the growing centrality of climate change and sustainable development, reflecting the increasing convergence of AI research with global sustainability priorities. BERTopic analysis further revealed eleven interpretable abstract-level thematic domains after excluding one heterogeneous outlier category. The dominant themes included digital transformation and green innovation, AI-enabled education, digital health, smart agriculture, renewable energy systems, clean water and sanitation, remote sensing, NLP-based decision support, sustainable construction, tourism, and sustainable chemistry/pharmaceutical applications. This study maps the AI–SDG research landscape by integrating bibliometric indicators with thematic evolution, conceptual analysis, and abstract-level semantic topic modelling. The findings provide insights into the development and thematic orientation of AI-related research in the context of sustainable development. The use of BERTopic complements conventional bibliometric approaches by examining semantic patterns within publication abstracts alongside keyword and citation-based analyses.

High-dimensional bioinformatics data, characterized by a large number of features relative to the number of samples, pose major challenges such as the ``curse of dimensionality,'' leading to overfitting, high computational cost, and poor generalization. Traditional feature selection methods often suffer from limited scalability and adaptability in such domains. We propose an LLM-in-the-loop reinforcement learning (RL) framework for bioinformatics feature selection, where the RL agent formulates feature selection as a sequential decision-making task, while the large language model (LLM) enhances the process in two ways: (1) guiding exploration through domain-informed advice, and (2) providing hybrid rewards that integrate data-driven performance with knowledge-driven evaluation. The LLM also produces explanations to improve interpretability for human experts without altering the RL policy update. Experiments on diverse bioinformatics datasets show that the LLM-in-the-loop framework outperforms baselines, achieves stable performance across downstream models, and converges faster than pure RL.

The modern business world is changing rapidly with the increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) and predictive analytics. Earlier, businesses depended mainly on past data to understand what had already happened. Today, AI and analytics help organizations predict future situations and make better decisions based on available data. This change has given rise to the idea of “augmented intelligence”, in which AI works together with people to support their decisions instead of replacing them. This paper studies how the use of AI and predictive analytics is affecting businesses and the way managers make decisions. It focuses on the use of AI in daily work, the automation of routine tasks, access to analytical tools and the changing role of human judgment in decision-making. A survey of 35 management professionals (N = 35) was conducted to understand their practical experience of AI and analytics in the workplace. The results show that AI is already being used in many professional roles: about 88.6% of respondents said that their work involves both AI and analytics, and 82.9% said that AI has significantly reduced their workload.

Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Roadside traffic reasoning requires every free-form textual claim to be backed by visual evidence. Existing grounded multimodal large language models (MLLMs) frequently exhibit say-point mismatch, in which the textual answer contradicts the bounding boxes the model localizes. Evaluation metrics that score answers and boxes separately leave this failure unpenalized. We trace the mismatch to the conventional answer-then-ground factorization, which commits to a numerical claim before any object is enumerated. To measure it, we build RoadSceneVQA-G, a benchmark of 34.7K question-answer pairs in which every free-form answer is linked to the set of boxes that witnesses it, and we propose the Answer-Grounding Consistency (AGC) evaluation suite. To address it, we introduce Enumerate-then-Answer (EtA), which reverses the generation order so that answer-evidence agreement becomes a property of the output structure, and Enumeration-Consistent Policy Optimization (ECPO), a reinforcement learning stage that uses the union of multiple rollouts as a recall teacher without ground-truth boxes. EtA raises say-point consistency from 26.6\% to 93.7\% and grounding F1 from 52.2\% to 73.0\%, and ECPO further increases F1 to 75.6\% without per-box supervision. On gRefCOCO, the same framework outperforms the strongest compared method, indicating that it transfers beyond traffic scenes. The project is available at \url{https://github.com/GuanRunwei/RoadSceneVQA-G}.

In the fast-changing digital education and the rapid development of artificial intelligence, AI-generated feedback has been widely used in college English writing assessment as a valuable teaching support. The traditional manual marking is typically characterized by a heavy workload, slow feedback, and subjective judgment, making it difficult to meet students’ individual needs for writing improvement. AI feedback can detect surface-level language errors and improve the efficiency of assessment because it can provide immediate feedback, follow standard correction procedures, and offer detailed diagnostic guidance, thereby helping students to revise their writing autonomously. In this study, the analysis of student essays titled “The Impact of Influencer Culture on Youth Consumption Patterns” will be done to evaluate the utility of feedback provided by artificial intelligence. Additionally, rule-based AI correction and a more detailed review by teachers considering the practical value and importance of the learning process will be applied. It is proved that AI is quite efficient when dealing with language mistakes, yet it is insufficient in the logical development of an essay, in-depth interpretation, and critical thinking that are still the responsibility of teachers. From the author’s teaching experience, a new model that combines the efforts of AI and teachers can be proposed, according to which AI makes surface-level corrections and teachers concentrate on developing the higher-order skills of students.

Embodied agents benefit from 3D environments that combine visual fidelity to real-world observations with physical interactivity. Existing single-image tabletop reconstruction methods recover plausible scene geometry but typically represent objects as monolithic rigid bodies, limiting interaction to whole-object rigid motion and precluding executable part-level articulation. Meanwhile, recovering a scene layout consistent with the input view remains challenging because a single observation may admit multiple plausible pose-scale configurations. We present ArticuTable, a single-image 3D tabletop reconstruction framework that recovers both executable part-level articulation and an input-view-consistent scene layout. For object modeling, we introduce generation-robust articulation modeling (GRAM), which combines joint fitting guided by a multimodal large language model with semantic state reasoning to recover reliable joint parameters and valid motion ranges from imperfect monolithic proxy meshes, thereby converting them into executable articulated assets. For scene layout, we introduce progressive semantic-geometric scene registration (PSGSR), which progressively narrows the pose-scale search space under complementary metric, planar, and input-view constraints and resolves orientation ambiguity through structure-aware semantic correspondences, yielding a scene layout consistent with the input view. We further contribute ArticuTable-100, a curated collection of 100 simulation-ready tabletop scenes. Extensive evaluation, including a user study, demonstrates strong performance across visual fidelity, input-view consistency, articulation quality, physical plausibility, and simulation readiness.

Artificial intelligence is fundamentally reshaping occupational medicine through applications in automation, smart monitoring, extended reality training, algorithmic management, and digital work arrangements. The EASOM Summer School 2025 examined how AI technologies enhance occupational health systems by enabling real-time risk identification, predictive surveillance, and targeted interventions to prevent work-related accidents and diseases. Practical applications include smart personal protective equipment, wearable sensors, augmented reality training systems, and predictive diagnostics exemplified by noise-related hearing loss risk assessment. However, significant challenges accompany these opportunities: data quality concerns, new technological hazards, psychosocial risks including surveillance-related stress and work intensification, algorithmic bias, and accountability gaps. Implementation requires comprehensive governance frameworks emphasizing early worker involvement, privacy-by-design approaches, phased pilot programs, and human-centered practices that complement rather than replace traditional occupational safety measures. Professional responsibility and education demand new competencies in digital literacy, algorithmic critical thinking, and applied ethics while maintaining essential clinical judgment and empathy. AI offers unprecedented potential for protecting workers' health and safety when responsibly implemented within transparent frameworks, but poor management risks deepening inequalities and eroding established protections. Successful integration depends on multidisciplinary research, international cooperation, stakeholder engagement, and a commitment to human-centered occupational medicine that prioritizes worker dignity and wellbeing.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces
Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: This systematic literature review examines the relationship between artificial intelligence (AI) anxiety and employee performance, with particular attention to job insecurity, threat–challenge appraisal, coping, career resilience, job crafting, leadership, training, organisational support, and human–AI collaboration. The review synthesises publicly accessible scholarly evidence and a supplied research corpus using multiple conceptual search strategies and backward and forward citation searching. The evidence is organised around two complementary pathways. The first is a threat pathway, in which AI-related concerns about job replacement, skill obsolescence, loss of autonomy, and employment continuity may contribute to anxiety, job insecurity, emotional exhaustion, withdrawal, and weaker performance-related outcomes. The second is an opportunity pathway, in which AI is appraised as a manageable challenge and can support learning, job crafting, adaptation, engagement, and performance when appropriate personal and organisational resources are available. The review integrates Cognitive Appraisal Theory, Conservation of Resources Theory, and Job Demands–Resources theory to explain why employee responses to AI differ across contexts. It identifies career resilience, AI self-efficacy, learning ability, training, supportive leadership, organisational support, employee participation, transparency, and human-centred AI governance as important potential buffers. A qualitative thematic synthesis is used because the included studies differ substantially in constructs, occupational settings, countries, research designs, and outcome measures. The review does not claim exhaustive coverage of proprietary bibliographic databases such as Scopus or Web of Science. No new human-participant data were collected. This work is released as a research preprint for open scholarly dissemination and future updating as additional database records become available.

Artificial intelligence may become an ordinary input into economic and civic life, accessed through services as routinely as electricity. This essay examines what that possibility means for India as it approaches the centenary of independence in 2047. Building on the argument of The Grid That Thinks, it uses the history of electrification and selected research on productivity, AI costs and infrastructure to assess the utility analogy. The central argument is that affordable computational capability produces broad social value only when institutions reorganise around it and access includes language, reliability, accountability and effective redress. The analogy illuminates complementary investment and unequal diffusion, but weakens when applied to the measurement of intelligence, market structure and systems that interpret information or act on users' behalf. The essay proposes a plural infrastructure approach combining shared public capabilities, competing providers, local evaluation and human fallback. It treats 2047 as a planning horizon rather than a forecast and identifies observable outcomes by which the promise of an intelligence utility could be judged.

Purpose Research on artificial intelligence (AI) in organisations has concentrated on operational efficiency and automation. This study aims to reposition AI as both a constitutive element and a strategic object of foresight, a dual role the literature has noticed but not theorised. Design/methodology/approach A narrative literature review draws peer-reviewed work from foresight studies, socio-technical systems theory and organisational change into an integrated analytical framework. Selection prioritised conceptual contribution, transparency of reasoning and relevance to AI in strategic futures thinking. Findings AI strengthens environmental sensing, complex modelling and scenario work under uncertainty. The framework has four components: inputs, AI systems, human–AI interaction and outcomes, and yields five propositions for empirical testing. Research limitations/implications As a theoretical contribution, empirical validation remains a priority. Findings should be tested across sectors and organisational contexts before generalisation. Practical implications Organisations must cultivate digital foresight literacy, restructure around cross-functional foresight teams and implement agile governance capable of auditing AI-generated outputs. The framework provides guidance for navigating algorithmic bias, transparency obligations and power asymmetries. Originality/value This study makes four contributions. It reconceptualises AI as constitutive of organisational foresight instead of an instrument applied to it, introduces and differentiates anticipatory co-evolution as a novel construct, integrates Rohrbeck’s (2010) maturity model with Ivanov’s (2023) configuration taxonomy and sets out ethical governance requirements specific to AI-enabled foresight.

Artificial intelligence is increasingly used to support spoken language practice. However, different AI-assisted support systems do not support learners’ confidence equally. This explanatory sequential mixed-methods study examines associations among the perceived usefulness of AI feedback, AI-mediated argumentative scaffolding, self-reported cognitive engagement, and speaking self-efficacy in the context of spontaneous argumentation. The quantitative phase involved 130 university EFL learners who had used an AI-assisted argumentation coaching application for at least eight weeks. Regression analysis showed that perceived usefulness of AI feedback was positively associated with so-called speaking self-efficacy, that is, the confidence to perform spoken tasks successfully (β = .410, p < .001), as was AI-mediated argumentative scaffolding (β = .248, p = .002). In contrast, self-reported cognitive engagement was not significantly associated with speaking self-efficacy after the other predictors were taken into account (β = −.028, p = .725). The qualitative phase involved eight purposively selected participants representing variation in gender, year of study, IELTS target, and experiences relevant to the quantitative patterns. Thematic analysis of semi-structured interviews identified three explanatory themes: structural scaffolding, psychological safety, and cognitive limits. Participants frequently described organizational guidance and a nonjudgmental practice environment as useful, while some also reported repetition, fatigue, and dependence during extended AI use. Integrating the two phases suggests that perceived usefulness, scaffolding, and cognitive engagement should not be treated as interchangeable dimensions of AI-assisted speaking practice. The study proposes a provisional cognitive-threshold hypothesis for future testing, but does not claim a causal or nonlinear effect. The findings support strategically designed AI-assisted speaking practice that maintains opportunities for independent reasoning and human interaction.

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative force in education and research, fundamentally reshaping teaching methodologies, learning experiences, and knowledge production in economics. This paper examines the role of AI in enhancing pedagogical practices, improving research efficiency, and redefining skill requirements in economics education. Drawing on recent empirical and theoretical literature, the study highlights key applications such as personalised learning, intelligent tutoring systems, data-driven research tools, and automated assessment. It also evaluates critical challenges including ethical concerns, academic integrity, digital inequality, and overreliance on AI systems. Empirically, the study utilised annual time series data from 2010 to 2024 and adopted the Autoregressive Distributed Lag (ARDL) model to analyse both short-run and long-run dynamics. Findings show that AI has a positive and statistically significant effect on learning outcomes in both the short run and long run. The paper concludes that while AI offers substantial opportunities for innovation in economics education and research, its successful integration requires strategic policy frameworks, ethical guidelines, and capacity building among educators and students.
